newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh Biharis join fast for Pakistan dream.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh Biharis join fast for Pakistan dream.

text.p: As Pakistan prepared to celebrate the golden jubilee of its independence, hundreds of its "forgotten" citizens began a fast in the Bangladesh capital Dhaka on Tuesday, saying they would rather die than give up their dream of going to Pakistan.

The hunger strikers were part of some 250,000 Biharis stranded in Bangladesh, formerly East Pakistan, after its civil war with West Pakistan in 1971. They were joined outside the National Press Club by Urdu-speaking Bihari women of all ages.
"We have been without a state for more than a quarter of a century. I have passed the prime time of my life keeping alive the dream that I will go home, eventually," said 40-year-old Noorjahan Begum.
"I have been married in an alien land (Bangladesh), my children have been born here, but I want my grave in Pakistan," she said.
The hunger strikers said the 24-hour fast was aimed at highlighting their plight and reinforcing their demand for repatriation to Pakistan.
"We would rather die than compromise on the issue (of repatriation)," one woman said.
"We planned the protest now to tell the world of our inhuman sufferings while our homeland (Pakistan) celebrates (its) 50th anniversary of independence.

"It's a shame on the part of Pakistan as hundreds of thousands of its citizens are left in another country without food, jobs or proper shelter, but with lots of humiliation," said the woman who declined to give her name.
Thousands of Urdu-speaking Moslems from the Bihar region of British-ruled India migrated to East Pakistan after the partition of the subcontinent in 1947.
When the Bengali-speaking eastern flank split from West Pakistan in 1971 to become Bangladesh, the Biharis were left without a nation.
They have since lived in 66 squalid camps in Dhaka and elsewhere in Bangladesh, awaiting their return to Pakistan.
The Biharis saw a ray of hope in 1992 when then Pakistan Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif began the repatriation process. Some 325 people made it to Pakistan in 1993.
But the repatriations stopped with the coming to power of Sharif's arch rival, Benazir Bhutto, the same year.
Now that Sharif is back in the prime minister's office, the Biharis -- their number now swollen to about 400,000 -- said they believed they might be able to go home soon.
The Bihari women on Tuesday hung portraits of Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and her slain father Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, who led Bangladesh to independence.
"Sheikh Hasina is aware of our sufferings. It's a tragedy to become stateless. We expect she would persuade Nawaz Sharif to take us home," one protester said.
Mohammad Nasim Khan, leader of the Stranded Pakistanis General Repatriation Committee, said that "not only Pakistan, the whole world has forgotten us".
Khan said the Biharis, who actively helped the Pakistan army during the 1971 war, were driven out of their houses, offices and factories in 1972.
"But we have since faced a stony silence from Pakistani authorities," he said recently.
India, which helped Bangladesh in the 1971 war, also celebrate its 50th independence anniversary on August 15.
But Bangladesh will mark the day with mourning for Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, who was killed with most of his family in an army coup on August 15, 1975.
